scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the Pays Plinn, dancers perform a fast, physical chain, often entering a 'tribal trance' by hammering the same relentless rhythm for hours, a practice Alan Stivell later fused with electric rock in 1971.
This is Plinn. Traditional, popularized in 1971.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (5JrqcsbHQ2c)
Title card: Plinn · France · Traditional, popularized in 1971

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Plinn originated in the Pays Fañch, south of the Côtes-d'Armor.
It is a traditional Breton dance that has been practiced for generations within the local fest-noz culture.
In 1971, Alan Stivell adapted the traditional air into a rock-influenced piece, which brought the dance and its music to a broader public.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Plinn is a social dance performed at community festivals.
It is associated with a 'tribal trance' state, achieved through the repetition of a relentless rhythm for hours.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Traditional accompaniment includes the biniou (Breton bagpipe) and the bombarde (a double-reed instrument).
The music is often accompanied by kan ha diskan, a traditional call-and-response singing style.
Listen for the Biniou, Bombarde, Electric guitar, Harp.
A fusion of traditional Breton melodies played on biniou and bombarde, often layered with electric guitar, harp, and steady percussion to create a driving, repetitive, and energetic sound.
